lesson.title: Silencing Messages After They Are Sent: MicroRNAs
lesson.summary: MicroRNAs are short non-coding RNA molecules that bind partially complementary sequences on target messenger RNAs, blocking their translation or triggering their degradation after transcription has already happened.
lesson.body:
Every regulatory mechanism covered so far, enhancers, silencers, DNA methylation, histone modification, and chromatin remodeling, works at the level of DNA and chromatin, controlling whether and how often a gene gets transcribed into messenger RNA in the first place. MicroRNAs, or miRNAs, operate at a completely different stage. They act after a messenger RNA transcript already exists, which is why this is called post-transcriptional regulation.

A microRNA starts out as a gene transcribed, like any other, into a long primary transcript called a pri-miRNA, which folds back on itself into a hairpin shape because parts of the single RNA strand are complementary to other parts of the same strand, an example of the base pairing within RNA structure covered earlier. An enzyme called Drosha trims this hairpin down to a shorter pre-miRNA, which is exported out of the nucleus and then cut again by an enzyme called Dicer into a mature miRNA duplex only about 21 to 23 nucleotides long. This step-by-step trimming of a longer RNA transcript into a shorter functional form echoes the general idea of mRNA processing covered earlier, just applied to a regulatory RNA instead of a message destined for translation.

One strand of the mature miRNA is loaded into a protein complex called RISC, the RNA-induced silencing complex, which uses the miRNA as a guide to find messenger RNAs with a complementary sequence, typically located in the mRNA's 3' untranslated region. The base pairing between miRNA and target does not need to be perfect. Once RISC is anchored on a target mRNA, it either physically blocks the ribosome from translating that message or recruits enzymes that degrade the mRNA outright, directly interrupting the translation process described in translation overview.

Because the base pairing only needs to be partial, a single microRNA can target many different messenger RNAs at once, letting one small molecule coordinate an entire program of gene expression changes, which is especially important during development and cell differentiation. Unsurprisingly, miRNAs that normally help restrain genes promoting cell division are found to be dysregulated in some cancers. With this, the survey of eukaryotic gene regulation and epigenetics is complete. The remaining sections shift focus from how cells naturally regulate their own genes to the laboratory tools scientists have built to read, cut, copy, and recombine DNA directly.
